topics.name: Grief & loss
topics.intro: A place to explore what loss means for you.
topics.article: There is no single story of loss
topics.question: What would you like to put into words about your loss?
topics.tool: A letter, if you feel like it
topics.toolBody: Write to a person, a part of your life, or yourself. There is no need to finish it, share it, or make it positive.

content.title: A place to begin.
content.lede: Whatever loss looks like for you.

cards.title: Some losses are hard to put into words.
cards.body: A death. A breakup. A friendship ending. Pregnancy loss. A change in your health, a role, or the future you imagined.
cards.note: Whatever you’re grieving, there is room to talk about it.

cards.eyebrow: When your sense of self shifts
cards.title: I don’t quite know who I am now.
cards.body: You may miss the life you shared, being needed, or the future you pictured. Parts of who you are may feel uncertain.
cards.note: Grief can touch your energy, concentration, relationships, and sense of purpose.

cards.eyebrow: You can start where you are
cards.title: I don’t know where to start.
cards.body: A counsellor can listen, help you explore what has changed, and work with you on what feels difficult right now.
cards.note: You can share as much or as little as you feel ready to. One sentence is enough to begin.

content.counsellorNote: You don’t need to have the right words. Start with what’s on your mind.

shorts.title: A gentler way into a hard conversation
shorts.try: I’ve been feeling ___ about ___. Could we find a time to talk it through?
frames: Start with one moment.
“When our plans changed yesterday, I felt out of the loop.” A specific moment can be easier to discuss than “you always” or “you never.”
Name what you need.
Try making a clear request: “Could we check with each other before changing our plans?” Leave room to hear their experience too.
Make room for a pause.
If either of you needs a break, agree on a time to return. The conversation can wait until you both feel ready.

shorts.title: Notice the little invitations
shorts.try: What is one small way you reach out to me that I might sometimes miss?
frames: “Look at this.”
A funny photo, a story from the day, a small sigh. Sometimes these are invitations for a little attention or connection.
Meet the invitation.
Put down what you’re doing for a moment, ask a question, or say “tell me more.” A response can be small and still thoughtful.
If now isn’t a good time…
You can say, “I want to hear this. Can we talk after I finish?” Then make a little room to come back.

shorts.title: Make a ritual that feels like you
shorts.try: What small tradition would feel like “us” and be easy to enjoy together?
frames: Begin with something ordinary.
Tea on the balcony. A song while cooking. A walk with no agenda. A shared ritual can be small.
Ask what it means to you.
Is this a moment of play, comfort, celebration, or belonging? You might each find something different in it.
Make it yours together.
Choose something you both want. Try it once, talk about how it felt, and change it as your lives change.

shorts.title: One small step toward a shared goal
shorts.try: What is one thing we both want to make more room for, and one small step we could try?
frames: Make room for both hopes.
Each share something you would like more of in the next few months. Listen before deciding what comes next.
Find a point of overlap.
A goal might be more rest, time together, learning something, or planning a trip. It should feel chosen by both of you.
Choose one small step.
Decide what feels manageable this week and who wants to do what. Pick a time to check in and adjust together.

means.W: Kind words land deepest: hearing that you are appreciated, admired, encouraged.
means.Q: Undivided attention is what feels like love: time together, phones down.
means.A: Help speaks loudest: a chore handled, a load lifted, a plan taken care of.
means.T: Closeness says it best: a hug, a hand held, sitting near each other.
means.G: A thoughtful gift, big or small, says “I was thinking of you.”

how.W: Say it out loud: what you admire, what you are grateful for. A text in the middle of the day counts.
how.Q: Plan time with nothing else in it. Put the phone away and ask about their day, then really listen.
how.A: Notice the chore they dread and do it before they ask. Take something off their plate this week.
how.T: A hug hello and goodbye, a hand on the shoulder, sitting close on the couch.
how.G: Small and personal beats big: their favourite snack, something they mentioned once.

statements: I often worry that the people I’m close to don’t care about me as much as I care about them.
I feel uncomfortable when someone wants to get very emotionally close to me.
If someone I love is distant or slow to reply, I assume something is wrong between us.
I find it easy to turn to people I’m close to for comfort and support.
I need a lot of reassurance that I’m loved and wanted.
I prefer not to depend on others, even when I’m struggling.
I worry about being abandoned or replaced.
It’s hard for me to open up about my feelings, even to people I trust.
I feel secure that the people close to me will be there when I need them.
When a relationship gets serious, I feel an urge to pull back or keep my space.

means.secure: Closeness and independence both feel fairly comfortable to you. You tend to trust that the people you love will be there, without needing a lot of reassurance.
means.anxious: Closeness matters a great deal to you, and you may sometimes wonder whether others care as much as you do. Small signs of distance can feel big, and reassurance helps you settle.
means.avoidant: You value your independence and like to handle things yourself. When someone wants a lot of emotional closeness, a little space can feel safer than leaning in.
means.fearful: You want closeness and also want to protect yourself from getting hurt, so you can feel pulled both ways: drawn toward people, then wanting some distance.

try.secure: Your steadiness helps you both. Keep saying what you feel and need out loud, so your partner never has to guess.
try.anxious: When worry starts, say it gently instead of watching for signs: “I’m feeling a bit unsure, can we check in?” Asking is allowed.
try.avoidant: When you need space, say so and say when you’ll be back: “I need an hour, then let’s talk.” It keeps the door open.
try.fearful: Notice the pull and the push without blaming yourself. Share one small feeling at a time, at a pace that feels safe.

pairs.secure+secure: You both tend to feel safe with closeness and with time apart. That gives you a steady base. Keep checking in, even when things feel easy.
pairs.secure+anxious: One of you tends to feel settled; the other can worry when things go quiet. Small, steady signs of care, like a quick message or keeping to plans, go a long way.
pairs.secure+avoidant: One of you is happy to lean in; the other likes room to breathe. Patience and an open door, without pressure, help closeness grow at its own pace.
pairs.secure+fearful: One of you tends to feel steady; the other can feel pulled between wanting closeness and wanting distance. Calm, predictable care helps trust build over time.
pairs.anxious+anxious: You both care deeply about closeness, and you can both worry when things feel uncertain. Reassure each other often, and say a worry out loud before it grows.
pairs.anxious+avoidant: When unsure, one of you reaches for closeness and the other looks for space. It is a common pattern, and it can turn into one following while the other steps back. Naming it together, kindly, takes much of the sting out.
pairs.anxious+fearful: You both feel things deeply and can both worry about getting hurt. Gentle reassurance and patience on both sides help you feel safe with each other.
pairs.avoidant+avoidant: You both value independence and room to breathe. That can feel easy, but feelings can also go unsaid. Make a little regular time to share how you’re really doing.
pairs.avoidant+fearful: You both tend to protect yourselves with some distance. Closeness may come slowly, and that is okay. Small, low-pressure moments of openness help.
pairs.fearful+fearful: You both want closeness and can both feel wary of it. Go gently, be patient with the push and pull, and notice the small moments of trust.

attachmentQuiz.gentle: A reflection tool, not a clinical assessment. Styles are tendencies, not labels: they can differ between relationships and change over time.

topics.intro: Finding your way through a new chapter.
topics.article: Making room for your needs, too
topics.question: What kind of support would feel useful to you this week?
topics.toolBody: Write down the practical help, company, or time you would appreciate. Then think about who you might ask.

content.title: You’re growing into this, too.
content.lede: For the beautiful, messy, still-figuring-it-out days.

stories.title: I love you. I miss parts of my old life.
stories.teaser: Making room for love and longing in the same day.
body: I found an old photo of myself getting ready to go out. Nothing special: a shirt I liked, music playing, nowhere urgent to be. I missed that version of an ordinary evening.
Then my baby made a tiny, ridiculous sound, and I laughed. Both feelings were there.

For a while, I thought missing my old life meant I wasn’t grateful enough for this one. Now I’m trying to describe what I miss more precisely: choosing my own pace, finishing a conversation, feeling like myself. I don’t have a neat answer. This week, I asked for an hour to do something familiar. It felt good to have that little space.

stories.title: I wanted someone to ask about me.
stories.teaser: One honest conversation beneath all the baby updates.
body: Every call began with the same lovely question: “How’s the baby?” I had plenty to say. New expressions, changing routines, another photograph. Somehow, by the end, I hadn’t said much about myself.
One afternoon, a friend asked, “And how has today been for you?” I almost gave my usual answer. Instead, I told her I felt stretched thin and a little lonely.

She didn’t turn it into advice. We talked about my day, then hers. Later, I sent another friend a message: “I’d love some company. Could we talk about something other than baby things for a while?” It was a small request, but it sounded like me.

stories.title: We’re getting to know each other.
stories.teaser: Finding connection in ordinary moments of care.
body: I imagined there would be a moment when I suddenly felt confident as a dad. Instead, there were lots of ordinary moments when I was learning.

I started talking to my baby while getting their clothes ready. Completely unremarkable things: the weather, a song stuck in my head, why I could never find the other sock. At first, I felt a bit silly.

Over time, this became something I looked forward to. I was learning their expressions and finding my own way to be present. I still have uncertain days. But caring for them gives us time together, and the other sock remains an excellent topic of conversation.

videos.title: A pause for tired days
videos.label: Feeling exhausted
frames: You can put something down.
For this moment, choose one thing that does not need to be finished right now.
What would help a little?
Company, practical help, a quieter room, or time to rest? Choose something that fits this day.
Give the need some words.
“Could you take care of ___ for a while so I can ___?” You can make the request small and specific.

videos.title: Nothing to do, for a moment
videos.label: Guided deep rest
frames: A little room to rest.
Choose a moment when your baby is safely cared for and you can pause. Find a comfortable, supported position.
Notice what is holding you.
The chair, the cushion, the bed. Let your breathing find its own pace. There is no task to complete here.
Return in your own time.
Notice the room around you. Take a little time before moving on to the next part of your day.

videos.title: When plans keep changing
videos.label: Finding a little control
frames: Some days won’t follow the plan.
Name one thing that feels uncertain today. You do not need to solve the whole day at once.
Look for one choice you have.
Could you simplify a task, postpone something, or ask someone to take one thing on?
Make the next step small.
Choose what feels manageable now. You can change the plan again when you need to.

videos.title: Making room for how you feel
videos.label: Understanding emotions
frames: Start with your own words.
Tired, tender, joyful, lonely, unsure — or something else entirely. What word fits this moment?
You don’t have to explain it away.
You can ask someone to listen without asking them to fix it. “Could I tell you how today has felt?”
Support can include a professional.
If changes in your mood feel persistent or worrying, talk with a health professional. You can ask for support without finding perfect words.

videos.title: Why everything can feel different
videos.label: Hormones & change
frames: A lot is changing.
After birth, hormonal changes, physical recovery, sleep, and new responsibilities can all be part of how you feel.
Your experience deserves attention.
Difficult feelings do not need to be dismissed as “just hormones.” There is room to talk about what is happening for you.
Bring your questions.
A health professional can help you understand changes and find support that fits. This video would be led by a perinatal clinician.

videos.title: Moving at your own pace
videos.label: Gentle postnatal movement
frames: Recovery is personal.
This planned video introduces gentle postnatal movement with a qualified postnatal clinician.
Start with what fits your recovery.
The right starting point depends on your birth and recovery. A clinician can help you choose suitable movements.
A guided session, when ready.
The final video would demonstrate clinician-selected movements and adaptations. Exercises are not demonstrated in this storyboard.

stretches.name: Palming & Reset
stretches.sub: Your eyes are muscles too — give them a moment of rest.
steps: Rub your palms together quickly until they feel warm.
Close your eyes and cup your warm palms gently over them.
Keep your eyes closed, slowly breathe for 30 sec. Open your eyes when you hear a ping.
Open your eyes. Trace a slow figure-eight in the air with your gaze.

stretches.name: Neck Release
stretches.sub: Unwind hours of desk tension in under two minutes.
steps: Sit tall. Slowly drop your right ear toward your right shoulder.
Hold for 3 deep breaths — feel the left side of your neck soften.
Roll your chin slowly down to your chest. Breathe.
Continue over to your left shoulder. Hold for 3 breaths.
Add 3 shoulder rolls forward, 3 back. Shake it out.

stretches.name: Shoulder Release
stretches.sub: Melt the tension you carry up around your ears.
steps: Roll both shoulders up toward your ears, then back and down — 5 slow rolls.
Reverse — roll them forward and down 5 times.
Bring your right arm across your chest; draw it in with your left hand. Hold 20 seconds.
Switch — left arm across your chest. Hold 20 seconds.
Reach both arms overhead, interlace your fingers and press your palms to the sky. Hold 3 breaths.

stretches.name: Full Spine Sequence
stretches.sub: Stretch your spine in every direction it can move.
steps: Flexion — round your spine forward, tuck your chin, draw your navel in. Hold 3 breaths.
Extension — arch back, lift your chest and gaze gently upward. Hold 3 breaths.
Side bend left — reach your right arm overhead and lean left. Hold 3 breaths.
Side bend right — reach your left arm overhead and lean right. Hold 3 breaths.
Rotation left — sit tall and twist gently to the left. Hold 3 breaths.
Rotation right — sit tall and twist gently to the right. Hold 3 breaths.
Return to centre and rest. Let your spine settle for 30 seconds.

stretches.name: Wrist Reset
stretches.sub: Essential for anyone who types or scrolls all day.
steps: Extend both arms in front of you, palms facing down.
Make slow circles with both wrists — 5 in each direction.
Shake your hands out loosely for 5 seconds.
Press your palms together at chest height.
Slowly lower your hands toward your waist, palms together. Hold 20s.

stretches.name: Legs Reset
stretches.sub: Your legs carry you everywhere — give them this.
steps: Sit at the very edge of your chair.
Straighten your right leg, heel resting on the floor.
Sit tall and hinge slowly forward from your hips — not your back.
Reach toward your foot. Hold 20 seconds, breathing deeply.
Switch legs. Repeat twice on each side.
Chair squats — stand in front of the seat, feet hip-width apart.
Lower slowly as if to sit, lightly tap the seat, then stand tall. Do 10 reps.
Stand and rest, hands on hips. Breathe for 20 seconds.

moods.label: Angry
moods.name: Long Exhale Breathing
moods.sub: A longer exhale switches on your calming response. Let each out-breath be slow and complete.

moods.label: Anxious
moods.name: Feet Press + Box Breathing
moods.sub: Four even sides. Ground through your feet while the breath moves around the box.
moods.note: Press both feet firmly into the floor — feel the ground hold you — as you breathe.

moods.label: Jealous
moods.name: Gratitude Pause
moods.sub: Comparison fades when your attention turns to what is already yours.
steps: Place one hand on your heart and take a deep breath.
Type one thing you are grateful for.
Type two more. Small and ordinary still count.
Sit with these for 30 seconds.
Carry that fullness with you.

moods.label: Can’t stop scrolling
moods.name: 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Reset
moods.sub: Pull your mind out of the feed and back into the room through your senses.
steps: Look around and name 5 things you can see.
Notice 4 things you can feel — your seat, your feet, the air.
Listen for 3 things you can hear.
Find 2 things you can smell.
Notice 1 thing you can taste. You are here now.

moods.label: Nervous
moods.name: Steady Seat Breathing
moods.sub: Let your body settle first, then a slow, even breath steadies you.
steps: Rest your back on the chair and place your feet on the ground.
Gently roll your shoulders back once, then let them drop.
Unclench your jaw.
Breathe gently in through your nose for 4 counts, then out through your mouth for 4. Repeat 5 times without holding or forcing your breath.

moods.label: Can’t switch off
moods.name: 4-6 Breathing
moods.sub: A short in-breath and a long out-breath ease you toward rest. Let it slow you all the way down.
